Albania.summary: Part of the Byzantine Empire, with Dyrrachium (Durrës), long the chief port of Roman Illyricum. The Avars took Sirmium in 582, and Slavs pushed into the Balkans; between the 6th and 8th centuries they settled and assimilated Illyrian tribes farther north, but the tribes of southern Illyria, including modern Albania, kept their own language. The large Komani cemetery (6th–8th centuries) attests a continuing local population.

events.t: The Avars capture Sirmium, a Balkan fortress; Slavs who besiege Sirmium and Singidunum in the 580s then push deep into the Balkans.
The large Komani cemetery in the north (6th–8th centuries) shows a local population persisting through the period.
A mutiny topples Emperor Maurice; afterwards the Byzantine Danube frontier crumbles and is not restored for centuries.

sources.title: Early Medieval North Albania: New Discoveries, Remodeling Connections. The Case of Medieval Komani
sources.publisher: Edizioni Ca' Foscari (Ca' Foscari University of Venice)

Belarus.polity: Baltic-speaking peoples, with Slavs pushing in (no state)
Belarus.summary: Archaeology shows the Bancer-Tushemlya culture (6th–8th centuries) on the upper Dnieper, upper Neman and Daugava, which most researchers attribute to Baltic tribes. People farmed and kept livestock, lived in open settlements, used hillforts as refuges, built small round sanctuaries, and cremated their dead, burying the remains under mounds. The culture declined under intensive Slavic expansion northward.

events.t: Bancer-Tushemlya culture (6th–8th centuries): open settlements, refuge hillforts, farming and stock-raising, and cremation burials under mounds.

Bosnia and Herz..polity: Former Roman province of Dalmatia; Avar pressure and Slav settlement
Bosnia and Herz..summary: Most of this land had belonged to the Roman province of Dalmatia, home to Illyrian tribes. After the Avars took Sirmium in 582, Slavs pressed into the Balkans; between the 6th and 8th centuries they settled here and assimilated the Illyrian population. Under Heraclius, Serb groups, earlier Avar vassals, settled inland of the Dalmatian coast, including eastern Herzegovina.

events.t: The Avars capture Sirmium; Slavs then infiltrate the western Balkans.
Serb groups, clients of Heraclius, settle inland of the Dalmatian coast, including eastern Herzegovina (date approximate).

Bulgaria.polity: Eastern Roman Empire (Thrace and the lower Danube), under Avar and Slav pressure
Bulgaria.summary: This was Roman Thrace and the lower Danube frontier, close to Constantinople. Slavs who had besieged Sirmium and Singidunum in the 580s pushed into the Balkans, and by the end of the century much of present-day Bulgaria was Slavicized. Emperor Maurice campaigned constantly and forced the Avars back across the Danube by 602, but his order for troops to winter beyond the river provoked the mutiny that made Phocas emperor. Afterwards the frontier crumbled.

events.t: After the Avar and Slav sieges of Sirmium and Singidunum in the 580s, Slavs push deep into the Balkans.
Maurice's armies campaign repeatedly in the Balkans, forcing the Avars back across the Danube by 602.
The Danube army mutinies over wintering north of the river; Phocas marches on Constantinople and Maurice is killed.
The Avars and their Slav allies, coordinating with a Persian army, besiege Constantinople and fail.

sources.title: Antes
sources.publisher: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies)

Croatia.polity: Roman province of Dalmatia, collapsing before Avars and Slavs
Croatia.summary: Roman Dalmatia had its chief city at Salonae, near Split. Avar and Slav pressure on the Balkans grew from the late 500s, and between the 6th and 8th centuries Slavs settled here and assimilated the older Illyrian population. After the Avars sacked the town in 615, its people built a new town inside Diocletian's palace at Split. Heraclius later allowed Croats who accepted Christianity to settle in the northwest Balkans.

events.t: The Avars sack Salonae; refugees build a new town inside Diocletian's palace at Split (c. 615).
Croats settle in the northwest Balkans with the permission of Heraclius, once they accept Christianity (date approximate).

Czechia.polity: Slavic tribes; probably part of Samo's realm (c. 623–658)
Czechia.summary: From the 6th century an early Slavic culture marked by Prague-type pottery spread across this region; ancient DNA from neighbouring Moravia shows a strong population shift between the 5th and 7th centuries. Many Slavs lived under Avar domination. In 623 or 624 a Frankish merchant named Samo was chosen king by Slavs (Wends) who rebelled against the Avars; he ruled until 658, and his realm included at least part of Bohemia. The main source is the Chronicle of Fredegar.

events.t: An early Slavic culture marked by Prague-type pottery spreads across the region (6th–early 7th century).
Samo is chosen king by the Slavs after their revolt against the Avars (623 or 624).
Samo's Slavs defeat the army of the Frankish king Dagobert I at Wogastisburg (date as given by Fredegar).

sources.title: Ancient genomes provide evidence of demographic shift to Slavic-associated groups in Moravia

Greece.polity: Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, with Slav settlement inland
Greece.summary: Greece was Greek-speaking, Christian Roman territory ruled from Constantinople. From the late 6th century many Slavs entered it, and together with the Avar wars they disrupted the economy: building of churches and secular works almost ceased, and newcomers reached deep into the Peloponnese. Inland, Slavic chieftaincies (sklaviniai) dominated many districts, while fortified cities with sea access, such as Thessalonica and Corinth, stayed in imperial hands.

events.t: Avars and Slavs besiege Thessalonica; a local miracle collection credits Saint Demetrius with saving the city.
Heraclius overthrows Phocas and becomes emperor.
Slav tribes attack Thessalonica (c. 620), and in 622 the Avars besiege it, according to the Miracles of Saint Demetrius.
Newcomers settle deep in the Peloponnese; the later, controversial Chronicle of Monemvasia describes Greek flight (dates disputed).

sources.title: The festival of Saint Demetrios, the Timarion, and the Aithiopika
sources.publisher: Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies (Cambridge University Press)

sources.title: Chronicle of Monemvasia, in A Guide to Byzantine Historical Writing

Hungary.polity: Avar Khaganate (heartland in the Carpathian Basin)
Hungary.summary: From 567–568 the Hungarian plain was the centre of the Avar Khaganate, a steppe power whose ruling elite was largely of East-Central Asian origin and which dominated Slavic peoples. The Avars took Sirmium in 582 and, between periods of Byzantine subsidies and tribute, pressed the Balkans until their failed siege of Constantinople in 626, after which their power waned. Rich 7th-century elite graves of the Kunbábony group reflect their wealth.

events.t: The Avars capture the Balkan fortress of Sirmium.
Phocas concludes a peace with the Avars, freeing troops for the Persian war.
Heraclius secures peace with the Avars by promising massive tribute payments.
An Avar host besieges Constantinople with Slav allies, coordinated with a Persian army; the assault fails.

sources.title: Genetic insights into the social organisation of the Avar period elite in the 7th century AD Carpathian Basin

Kosovo.polity: Eastern Roman Empire (Dardania), giving way to Slav settlement
Kosovo.summary: This was part of the Roman province of Dardania, whose city of Ulpiana Justinian, a native of the region, rebuilt as Justiniana Secunda. Avar and Slav pressure on the Balkans grew from the 580s, and after 602 the Danube frontier crumbled. Archaeologists now question the old view that Avar and Slav attacks quickly emptied Ulpiana. Slavs settled widely in the central Balkans during the 7th century.

events.t: After Avar and Slav sieges on the Danube in the 580s, Slavs push deep into the central Balkans.
Mutiny on the Danube topples Maurice; afterwards the Balkan frontier crumbles.

sources.title: Mosaic Inscription Connects Justinian to Ancient City in Kosovo

Macedonia.polity: Eastern Roman Empire, with growing Slav settlement
Macedonia.summary: This upper Vardar region lay in the Roman provinces of Macedonia. Stobi, an episcopal seat and capital of Macedonia Secunda, was abandoned in the last decade of the 6th century. Avar and Slav raids hit the Balkans from the 580s, and many Slavs settled here; those of Macedonia kept their Slavic speech. The empire held Thessalonica to the south.

events.t: Avars and Slavs besiege Thessalonica, the great city to the south.
Stobi is abandoned during the last decade of the 6th century.

sources.title: Taking care of an archaeological site (Stobi)
The festival of Saint Demetrios, the Timarion, and the Aithiopika
sources.publisher: Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies (Cambridge University Press)

Moldova.polity: Slavic communities within the range of the Antes, under Avar pressure
Moldova.summary: Slavs arrived in this land between the Prut and Dniester in the 6th century, though invasions disrupted their settlement. The Antes, an eastern Slavic tribal alliance centred between the Dnieper and Dniester, at times extended across the forest-steppe to the lower Danube. The Avars passed through Antes lands about 560, and from the late 500s the Antes fought them stubbornly.

events.t: Wars with the Avars break up the Antes alliance; Byzantine writers stop mentioning the Antes in the early 7th century.

sources.title: Antes
sources.publisher: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies)

Montenegro.polity: Former Roman Illyricum, giving way to Slav settlement
Montenegro.summary: Before the Slavs arrived in the 6th and 7th centuries, the area was inhabited mainly by Illyrians, whom modern Albanians claim as ancestors, and Rome had ruled Illyria for some six centuries. Between the 6th and 8th centuries Slavs settled widely and assimilated Illyrian tribes. Under Heraclius, Serb groups settled inland of the Dalmatian coast, across northern Montenegro.

events.t: Serb groups, clients of Heraclius, settle inland of the Dalmatian coast, including northern Montenegro (date approximate).

Poland.polity: Slavic and other tribal communities (no state)
Poland.summary: When Slavs reached this region is debated: one view holds that they arrived no earlier than the 6th century, another that they lived here since the Iron Age. After the Migration Period, material cultures across the region became more homogeneous, and archaeologists link them with the Slavs. These people cremated their dead, which makes their origins hard to test with ancient DNA.

events.t: Material cultures across the region grow more homogeneous, a change archaeologists link to Slavs (date of their arrival debated).

sources.title: Genetic history of East-Central Europe in the first millennium CE
Ancient genomes provide evidence of demographic shift to Slavic-associated groups in Moravia

Romania.polity: Slavs and Avars north of the Danube; Byzantine frontier on the river
Romania.summary: North of the lower Danube lived Slavic groups, many subject to the Avars, who raided and then settled south of the river. Emperor Maurice campaigned constantly in the Balkans and forced the Avars back across the Danube by 602, but that year his order for soldiers to winter in enemy lands beyond the river caused a mutiny that toppled him. After 602 the Danube frontier crumbled.

events.t: Maurice's armies campaign along and across the Danube against Avars and Slavs.
Maurice orders the army to winter north of the Danube, triggering the mutiny that topples him.

sources.title: Antes
sources.publisher: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies)

Russia.polity: Western Turkic power in the south, from which the Khazars later emerged; Kubrat's Bulgars (c. 635)
Russia.summary: The southern steppe and north Caucasus lay under the Western Turks. Later texts call them Khazars, but the Khazars become distinguishable from their Western Turkic masters only by the 650s. In 627–628 Western Turkish forces allied with Heraclius stormed Darband and besieged Tiflis. As Western Turkish rule broke up, the Bulgar ruler Kubrat led a successful revolt about 635 and organized the confederation called Great Bulgaria.

events.t: Western Turkish forces allied with Heraclius storm Darband and besiege Tiflis (627–628); later sources call them Khazars.
Kubrat leads a successful Bulgar revolt and organizes Great Bulgaria (date disputed).

Serbia.polity: Eastern Roman Empire (Danube frontier), contested by Avars and Slavs
Serbia.summary: This was the Danube frontier of the Roman Empire, with Singidunum and nearby Sirmium. Justiniana Prima (Caričin Grad), built by Justinian near his birthplace, was an archbishopric seat. Avar and Slav sieges in the 580s broke the frontier, which crumbled after 602. The Serbs, first recorded as vassals of the Avars, became clients of Heraclius and settled inland, into southeastern Serbia.

events.t: Sirmium falls to the Avars.
Slavs successfully besiege Singidunum during the sieges of the 580s.
Mutiny on the Danube topples Maurice; afterwards the frontier crumbles.
Justiniana Prima (Caričin Grad) is abandoned under Heraclius amid Slavic invasions (date approximate).

sources.title: Caričin Grad – Iustiniana Prima, archaeological site (Tentative List)

Slovakia.polity: Slavs under Avar rule; possibly part of Samo's realm (c. 623–658)
Slovakia.summary: By the 6th century Slavs lived between the Avar Khaganate in the Carpathian Basin and the Frankish kingdom, many under Avar domination. In 623 or 624 Samo, a Frankish merchant, became king of Slavs (Wends) who had revolted against the Avars; Slovakia is among the proposed centres of his realm. Ancient DNA from neighbouring Moravia points to a population shift linked with Slavic expansion.

events.t: Samo is chosen king by the Slavs after their revolt against the Avars (623 or 624).
Samo defeats the army of the Frankish king Dagobert I at Wogastisburg (date as given by Fredegar).

sources.title: Ancient genomes provide evidence of demographic shift to Slavic-associated groups in Moravia

Slovenia.summary: Slavs, ancestors of the Slovenes, settled here in the 500s and over the following centuries assimilated the older Illyrian population. The Slavs who pressed into the eastern Alps lived under Avar rulers and struggled with the Bavarians to the west. From about 623 a Slavic kingdom under Samo emerged that extended from the Sava valley northward.

events.t: Slavs under Avar rulers spread into the eastern Alps, at their greatest extent reaching Carinthia, Styria and Lower Austria.
Samo's Slavic kingdom forms, reportedly extending from the Sava valley northward.

Ukraine.polity: Antes and other Slavs; Pontic steppe peoples; Kubrat's Bulgars (c. 635)
Ukraine.summary: The Antes, an eastern Slavic tribal alliance between the Dnieper and Dniester, farmed with iron ploughs and were skilled potters and ironworkers. In the 6th century they joined Slavic raids on the Byzantine Balkans. The Avars passed through their lands about 560, and from the late 500s the Antes fought them stubbornly; the alliance broke up, and the Antes vanish from Byzantine writings in the early 7th century.

events.t: Wars with the Avars break up the Antes alliance; Byzantine writers stop mentioning them in the early 7th century.
Kubrat leads a successful Bulgar revolt and organizes Great Bulgaria (date disputed).
